01.event: In an incident, Rabbi acted in accordance with the Rabbis of the mishna
01.turn: Perata objected that the court would then have no advantage over an ordinary person
01.outcome: Rabbi reversed his action (or, in Rav Safra's version, refrained from acting)
01.summary: In an incident, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi acted according to the Rabbis' view. Perata, grandson of Rabbi Perata the Great, objected that this would leave the court no more power than an ordinary person. Rabbi reversed the action. Rav Safra's version has him only wishing to act, and then not acting.
01.missing: The incident itself (what the case was) is only alluded to
01.reason: There is an act, an objection and a reversal, which is a change. But the underlying incident is only alluded to and the exchange is mainly a ruling and speech, so it is part of a story rather than a full one.

02.event: The couple, admitting the levirate marriage was not consummated, came before Rava
02.turn: Rava ordered halitza; Rav Sherevya cited a baraita requiring a bill of divorce too
02.summary: A couple came before Rava, and he ruled that they should arrange halitza. Rav Sherevya objected with a baraita, and Rava withdrew his ruling.
02.missing: Any narrated action beyond coming before the rabbi and the ruling
02.reason: A case is brought before a rabbi and ruled on, then the ruling is debated. Coming before him is the only event, and the retraction is speech, so under R-C0's limit this is not a story.

03.missing: Any narrated event; the balcony is cited only as the subject of a lifelong dispute
03.reason: Abaye and Rava disagreeing about a balcony is cited as legal evidence. Nothing happens beyond their scholarly dispute.

04.event: His daughter married his brother Abba, who died childless
04.turn: Rabban Gamliel entered levirate marriage with her rival wife
04.outcome: The Gemara questions how a follower of Beit Hillel could do this
04.summary: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba. Abba died childless, and Rabban Gamliel took her rival wife in levirate marriage. The Gemara cites this as proof and then questions it.
04.missing: Any development or consequence; the incident is cited as a precedent
04.reason: There are real events (a death, then a levirate marriage) that respond to each other. But it is told only as a precedent for a legal proof, with no further development, so it is part of a story at most.

05.event: Hearing Rav Beruna cite Shmuel, he doubted it and asked to be shown Shmuel's lodging
05.turn: He went to Shmuel, who confirmed the ruling; Rabbi Elazar challenged him with Shmuel's own principle
05.summary: Rav Beruna was reciting a ruling of Shmuel. Rabbi Elazar doubted it, had Rav Beruna show him Shmuel's lodging, and went to ask Shmuel himself. Shmuel confirmed it. Rabbi Elazar confronted him with his own contrary statement, and Shmuel fell silent.
05.reason: It is mainly dialogue, but there are actions (being shown the lodging, going to Shmuel) and a confrontation that leaves Shmuel silent. It is mainly speech with some events, which is R-C7 shape 1.

06.missing: Any narrated event beyond an instruction
06.reason: Rav Pappa's instruction to Pappa the ox herder is a ruling cited as precedent. Nothing follows from it.

07.actor: The people of Bireta DeSatya; Rabbi Ahai son of Rabbi Yoshiya
07.event: A ditch of fish overflowed and they trapped the fish on Shabbat
07.summary: On his deathbed, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi named places in Babylonia. Of Bireta DeSatya he said that today they had turned away from God. A ditch of fish had overflowed and they trapped the fish on Shabbat. Rabbi Ahai excommunicated them, and they became apostates.
07.reason: Embedded in Rabbi's deathbed statement is a full incident: a sin, an excommunication, and a change (apostasy), linked by cause. The deathbed setting is itself an event.

08.event: They disagreed over liability in three cases
08.turn: Each jumped up and swore by the Temple service that he had heard his view from Rabbi
08.outcome: Each argued his case; the Gemara then analyzes the dispute
08.summary: Rabbi Hiyya and bar Kappara disagreed over three cases of double liability. In each, both jumped up and swore by the Temple service that their view came from Rabbi, and then each argued it out. The rest is the Gemara's analysis of their dispute.
08.missing: Any resolution or change; segments 8-15 are the Gemara's analysis
08.reason: It is mainly speech, but there is real conflict, with dramatic oaths and jumping up, and no change. Under R-C2 that makes it borderline, and the analysis after it is commentary, not story.

09.event: They carried a woman out on a bier
09.summary: As evidence that a woman may not be secluded even with ten dissolute men, Rav cites an incident in which ten men carried a woman out on a bier, pretending she was dead.
09.missing: The incident is only alluded to; its content has to be filled in from the commentary
09.reason: An incident only alluded to as legal evidence, which a reader can only reconstruct with outside help, is borderline under R-C6.

10.missing: Any event beyond a question and answer
10.reason: Rav Yirmeya asks Rav whether he has accepted the sanctity of Shabbat, and Rav says yes. That is a question and answer with no conflict.

11.missing: Any event beyond finding scholars debating
11.reason: Rav Nahman finding two scholars debating in the marketplace is a setting that frames a halakhic exchange. As in Shabbat 147a, a setting plus discussion is not a story.

12.missing: Any narrated event; the illness is supplied by the translator
12.reason: Rav Yosef says he never heard the ruling and Abaye reminds him that he taught it. This is ordinary scholarly dialogue with no event.

13.event: Rav Safra raised objections to Abaye's teaching
13.turn: Abaye was silent and went to Rav Yosef
13.outcome: Rav Yosef told him the answer he should have given
13.summary: Rav Safra challenged Abaye's teaching. Abaye answered the first objection and was silent at the second. When he came before Rav Yosef and reported it, Rav Yosef told him the answer he should have given.
13.missing: Any event or change beyond the dialogue
13.reason: Objections and answers between scholars are standard Talmudic discourse. Going to one's teacher only frames more dialogue, so there is no conflict or change in R-C2's sense.

14.actor: A certain man; Rav Shimi bar Hiyya
14.event: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags
14.turn: Rav Shimi examined whether it was worth a peruta
14.outcome: The Gemara reconciles the ruling with Shmuel
14.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags. Rav Shimi bar Hiyya examined it to decide whether the betrothal was valid, and the Gemara then reconciles this with Shmuel's view.
14.missing: Any outcome or further action beyond the ruling
14.reason: One event, a case brought for a ruling, and then legal discussion with nothing changing. Under Jeff's 2026-10-25 limit on R-C0 this is not a story.

15.missing: Any event beyond missing the study hall and asking what was said
15.reason: Rabbi Eliezer missing the study hall and asking Rabbi Asi what was said is a setting plus a question and answer, which is not a story (Shabbat 147a).

16.event: Rava coerced the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami
16.outcome: He collected four hundred zuz from him for charity
16.summary: Rava compelled Rav Natan bar Ami, a wealthy man, to give to charity, and collected four hundred zuz from him.
16.missing: Context, a response or any development; it is cited as a precedent
16.reason: It is a bare precedent, but the ruling is itself an act that changes something: coercion and collecting money. As in Ketubot 65a, that keeps it borderline rather than not.

17.actor: Rami bar Hama's sister and Rav Avya
17.turn: They came before Rav Yosef, who first said the Rabbis allow living without one; Abaye objected
17.outcome: Rav Yosef told him to write her a new one
17.summary: Rami bar Hama's sister, married to Rav Avya, lost her marriage contract. The couple came before Rav Yosef, who cited the Rabbis' leniency. Abaye objected, and Rav Yosef said: then go and write her one.
17.missing: Whether the new contract was written; anything after the ruling
17.reason: One event (the loss), then a case before a rabbi, discussion and a ruling. The outcome is only implied by an order, which Jeff said on 2026-10-25 does not count, so it is not a story.

18.event: Serving drinks at his son Abba Mar's wedding, he poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda
18.turn: Rav Yitzhak did not stand before him
18.summary: Rav Pappa was serving drinks at the wedding of his son Abba Mar. When he poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda, Rav Yitzhak did not stand before him, and Rav Pappa became angry.
18.reason: A one-time incident with actions (pouring, failing to stand) and an emotional reaction caused by them. Emotions count as events, so this is a minimal story, though it is cited as evidence.

19.event: He went up to Eretz Yisrael, was ordained, and was appointed to the intercalation council
19.turn: At each step he declared he had been spared one more curse
19.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael he said he had been spared one curse. When he was ordained he said two, and when he was appointed to the intercalation council, three.
19.missing: Causality or drama linking the events
19.reason: There are real events and a change in status, each with his response. But causality is weak and there is little drama, which is R-C7 shape 3.

20.event: Rav Beivai told the Sages not to listen to Rav Yosef's attribution, since he himself had taught it to him in another name
20.outcome: Rav Yosef exclaimed that he had confused 'Rabbi' with 'rabbim'
20.summary: Rav Beivai told the Sages to ignore Rav Yosef's version, because he had taught it to Rav Yosef in Rav Adda bar Ahava's name. Rav Yosef exclaimed, 'Master of Abraham!', and realized he had misheard 'rabbim' as 'Rabbi'.
20.reason: It is all speech: a correction about the source of a teaching, and an acknowledgment. Correcting a transmission is ordinary scholarly discourse rather than conflict in R-C2's sense.
